INTRODUCTION
The government asks this Court to stay a preliminary injunction so that it may
immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border bar-
rier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally
significant landscapes in the United States. A wilderness landscape that has re-
mained largely unscathed through the ages, the Big Bend region lies in the heart of
the Chihuahuan Desert and is defined by deep canyons, sheer cliffs, and rugged
mountain ranges. Its formidable terrain, harsh desert environment, and lack of roads
have long served as a natural barrier to travel through the region.
If granted, the requested relief would result in the permanent alteration of an
irreplaceable landscape that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State
Park, and nearly 200 miles of the congressionally designated Rio Grande Wild and
Scenic River corridor. A stay would likewise threaten unique historic and cultural
resources (including the Ruidosa Church), myriad private ranchlands, and other
property owners before the constitutionality of the challenged Waivers1 has been fi-
nally adjudicated. As highly destructive activities were already underway, the dis-
trict court entered its injunction to preserve the status quo and prevent further irrep-
arable harm during the brief period necessary to resolve the merits on pending sum-
mary judgment motions. As the district court recognized, if construction proceeds and

2
Respondents ultimately prevail, this beloved landscape and Respondents’ livelihoods,
recreation, and enjoyment “will have been forever altered.” App. 236a.
 That conclusion followed extensive briefing and an evidentiary hearing at
which Applicants declined to call a single witness, introduce any evidence, or other-
wise develop the factual record supporting the claims of purported urgency they now
advance. See Appl. 26–31; infra 11–13. Based on the evidence before it, the district
court found that the challenged construction has already harmed and, without in-
junctive relief, would irreversibly harm Respondents’ livelihoods, obstruct access to
the Rio Grande, fragment wildlife habitat, and otherwise impair the ecology of the
region by altering hydrologic function, damaging vegetation and fragile desert soils,
and inflicting ecological injuries that would persist for “decades if not centuries,” if
not in perpetuity. App. 237a. The court likewise found serious, irreparable injuries to
Respondents and the public at large from loss of wilderness that benefits tourism,
recreation, farming, ranching, education, and many other concrete interests. App.
215a–217a. Those factual findings are entitled to substantial deference.
Against those irreparable injuries, the district court expressly found that the
government would only suffer a “temporary delay” while the merits are assessed.
App. 217a. After entry of the injunction, the government offered new declarations in
attempting to substantiate its harm. App. 218a, 225a. But even its new submissions
identify the apprehension of just 18 individuals over a period of years, only some of
whom were alleged to have crossed in Big Bend. App. 227a–232a. As the district court
found, the broader record demonstrates that the Big Bend Sector experiences, by far,

3
the lowest apprehension rates anywhere on the southern border, with rates lower
than even the northern border’s Buffalo Sector. See App. 213a.
Indeed, Applicants themselves previously concluded that a similar delay would
not harm them. After construction began in Big Bend National Park, and following a
bipartisan groundswell of intense opposition, Applicants voluntarily paused construc-
tion across a vast portion of the project area for weeks. App. 221a. That voluntary
pause cannot be reconciled with Applicants’ present insistence that emergency relief
while the district court makes a final determination on the merits is necessary.
Applicants’ claims of harm are further undermined by unrebutted evidence
that border security operations in the Sector remain supported by extensive and ef-
fective surveillance technology, patrols, sensors, drones, and existing infrastructure.
Supp. App. 222a–225a; App. 33a–34a. Applicants also remain free to pursue desired
infrastructure projects by complying with the same laws that apply to agencies
throughout the country. App. 202a. And even further undercutting Applicants’ claim
of urgency is this case’s procedural posture. Summary judgment briefing is pending,
and the injunction merely preserves the status quo during time necessary for the
district court to resolve the constitutionality of Applicants’ extraordinary assertion
that Congress has authorized a single Executive Branch official to unilaterally dis-
pense with all statutory safeguards for landowners, businesspeople, and other ad-
versely affected members of the public across the entire border.
Nor have Applicants shown a likelihood of success on the merits. This case
involves an unprecedented assertion of executive authority by the U.S. Secretary of

4
Homeland Security (the “Secretary”). The Secretary claims power under the Illegal
Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (“IIRIRA”), Pub. L.
No. 104-208, Div. C, 110 Stat. 3009-546 (Sep. 30, 1996) (codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1103
note), as amended, Supp. App. 1a, to waive dozens of federal laws—and all “related”
state, local, and tribal laws—across approximately one-third of the U.S.-Mexico bor-
der. See App. 1a, 4a, 6a; Supp. App. 16a, 19a, 124a. The Waivers follow a series of
nine decisions in October 2025, waiving dozens of procurement laws for barrier con-
struction spanning the entirety of the U.S.-Mexico border. Supp. App. 5a. The Secre-
tary’s newfound view that Section 102’s waiver authority may be stretched to fiat
construction of a continent-spanning border barrier from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf
of America is a quintessential major question.
The Secretary’s assertion of authority is profound. Yet Congress limited
IIRIRA’s waiver authority to facilitating construction designed to “deter illegal cross-
ings in areas of high illegal entry.” 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a) note. As the district court found,
the Big Bend Sector has “the lowest rate of illegal entry along the entire U.S.-Mexico
border.” App. 214a. And as the court explained, “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of
high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to
the entire U.S.-Mexico border.” App. 214a. To be sure, Congress has considered au-
thorizing IIRIRA waiver authority across the entire border but declined to do so. See
infra 8.
Here, it is undisputed that the Waivers are of major economic and political
significance. App. 211a. Whatever authority Congress delegated, it did not clearly

5
authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here, and Applicants’ actions there-
fore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine. Under that
doctrine, decisions of such consequence belong to Congress, not a single Executive
Branch official.
There is likewise no merit to the government’s request that the Court grant
certiorari and summarily reverse. Not only have Applicants failed to cite any perti-
nent precedent for that extraordinary request, but the district court’s preliminary
ruling does not warrant this Court’s review in any event. Accordingly, the Court
should preserve the status quo and deny Applicants’ request to stay the preliminary
injunction, as well as their extraordinary request for certiorari and summary reversal
before judgment.
STATEMENT
I.
The Big Bend Region: A Great American Landscape
The Big Bend region is one of the most remote, rugged, and unique stretches
of land in the country—defined by its tightknit communities, working ranches, deep
canyons, rugged mountain ranges, vast public lands, dark skies, abundant archeolog-
ical and historic sites, unique biodiversity, and remarkable stretches of the Rio
Grande’s wild and scenic river. The region’s extraordinary and globally significant
natural, cultural, aesthetic, and human values led to its designation as the Big Bend
Biosphere Region by UNESCO in 1976. The region encompasses the largest intact

6
portion of the Chihuahuan Desert in the U.S. and is one of the world’s most biologi-
cally rich and diverse desert ecoregions.2
Big Bend National Park, “one of the wildest places in the Lower 48,” sits at the
heart of the region. App. 40a. It encompasses a “deceptively complicated terrain”
shaped by canyons reaching 1,500 feet in depth and mountains rising to 7,800 feet,
as well as steep cliffs, and hazardous, fragile vegetation unique to the Chihuahuan
Desert. App. 39a. On the Mexican side of the border, the terrain is similar, but even
vaster and more difficult to traverse. Id. Big Bend forms part of the largest trans-
boundary protected area in North America: more than three million acres of Chihua-
huan Desert and 200 miles of river are protected by the United States and Mexico.3
“Simply put, it’s the most wild, intact, unspoiled and hard-to-reach place left any-
where along the 2,000-mile U.S.-Mexico border.” Supp. App. 89a.
West of the National Park lies Big Bend Ranch State Park, the largest state
park in Texas. Supp. App. 73a. The Park’s dramatic geology offers a unique window
into the development of the North American continent, with rock formations uplifted
millions of years ago, volcanic events that formed mountains in the heart of the park,
and the Rio Grande continuing to shape the landscape along its southern boundary
through a process that began some 25 million years ago.4 To the east of the National
Park lies the mountainous Black Gap Wildlife Management Area, providing

Starting upriver from Mariscal Canyon in the National Park and ending at the

and recreational values.” Supp. App. 120a; see also 16 U.S.C. §§ 1271, 1274(a)(17).
Those who visit are rewarded with “the clearest spring-fed waters and most dramatic
canyon scenery in the Big Bend Region.” Supp. App. 136a. This stretch of river, bor-
dered by canyon rims rising over 1,000 feet, is renowned for its wildlife viewing and
recreational opportunities, particularly in the Lower Canyons, “the crème de la
crème” of the river corridor. App. 41a, 167a.
The region is cherished by a remarkably diverse community of people: hunters,
anglers, ranchers, conservationists, indigenous communities, historic preservation-
ists, paddlers, birders, and other outdoor enthusiasts. From a beloved golf course sit-
uated on the borderlands to miles of the Rio Grande, its lands and waters support
livelihoods, tourism, recreation and a way of life deeply rooted in a region unlike an-
ywhere else in the country. See, e.g., Supp. App. 156a3157a.
II.
Legal Background
IIRIRA Section 102 directs the Secretary to install physical barriers in the
“vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal
entry.” 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a) note (emphasis added). To support that important but
limited authority, Congress also conferred on the Secretary the waiver power in
IIRIRA Section 102(c)(1), providing the “authority to waive all legal requirements

8
such Secretary, in such Secretary’s sole discretion, determines necessary to ensure
expeditious construction of the barriers and roads under this Section.” 8 U.S.C.
§ 1103(c)(1) note.
Outside of IIRIRA Section 102, the Secretary maintains authority to construct
border barriers based on the general statutory responsibility to “guard the boundaries
and borders of the United States against the illegal entry of aliens.” Immigration and
Nationality Act, Pub. L. No. 82-414 § 103(a)(5) (1952), 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a)(5). That
authority exists independent of IIRIRA Section 102 and is unaffected by the district
court’s injunction.
III.
The Big Bend Waivers
For years, the United States has been embroiled in an “extensive, and often
intense” debate about whether our southern border should be barricaded by a wall.
California v. Trump, 379 F. Supp. 3d 928, 936 (N.D. Cal. 2019). In 2023, this debate
reached Congress—where both houses considered bills that would have authorized
the Secretary’s IIRIRA waiver authority to encompass the entirety of the U.S.-Mexico
Border. H.R. 2, 118th Cong. (2023); S. 2824, 118th Cong. (2023). That legislation did
not pass. Undeterred, then-Secretary Noem attempted to get there on her own. On
October 15, 2025, she issued nine new waiver determinations pursuant to IIRIRA
Section 102(c), waiving dozens of procurement laws for barrier construction along the
southern border (the “Procurement Waivers”).5 Each waiver encompasses the totality
5
The “Procurement Waivers” are: 90 Fed. Reg. 48281, 48282, 48283, 48284, 48285,
48286, 48287, 48288, 48289 (Oct. 15, 2025), Supp. App. 5a.

9
of a border patrol sector and, for the first time, span the entirety of the U.S.-Mexico
border. Supp. App. 109a.
Between February and July 2026, then-Secretary Noem and Secretary Mullin
issued another series of IIRIRA waivers that span approximately 607 miles of the
U.S.-Mexico border and make up the Big Bend Waivers at issue. See Supp. App. 73a.
The Waivers cover the entirety of the Big Bend Sector—an area that amounts to
around one quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, App. 75a, 95a, and now stretch into
the Del Rio Sector, encompassing one-third of the southern border. App. 95a; Supp.
App. 124a. In issuing each of the Waivers, the Secretary asserted that this area is
one “of high illegal entry” and that “Border Patrol apprehended over 89,000 illegal
aliens attempting to enter the United States between border crossings in the Big
Bend Sector” over a five-year period. App. 2a, 4a, 7a; Supp. App. 18a, 20a.
To rapidly construct “additional physical barriers and roads,” the Waivers
eliminate compliance with dozens of laws, including bedrock federal environmental
protection statutes (such as the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Safe Drinking Water
Act, and Endangered Species Act) as well as laws designed to protect historic re-
sources, Native-American artifacts and other cultural interests, farmland, private
property, and virtually all natural or human resources otherwise protected by law.
App. 1a, 4a, 6a; Supp. App. 16a, 19a. The Waivers also sweep within their scope all
“state, or other laws, regulations, and legal requirements, deriving from, or related
to the subject” of the enumerated federal statutes. Ibid. All of these legal safeguards
are waived “in their entirety, with respect to the construction of physical barriers and

10
roads,” which includes, “but [is] not limited to,” roads for “accessing the project areas,”
“earthwork, excavation, fill, and site preparation,” and “installation and upkeep of
physical barriers, roads, supporting elements, drainage, [and] erosion controls.” Ibid.
IV.
The Proceedings Below
On April 16, 2026, Plaintiff-Respondents filed suit in the U.S. District Court
for the Western District of Texas, challenging the Secretary’s waiver determinations
in Big Bend. D. Ct. Doc. 1. Respondents later amended and supplemented their com-
plaint to challenge additional Big Bend waivers. Supp. App. 22a. In addition to claim-
ing that the waivers constitute a “violation of the major questions doctrine under the
U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 1,” Supp. App. 57a, the operative Complaint
claims that, “in the alternative,” granting complete discretion to one executive branch
official to discard any and all federal statutes—along with any “related” state, local,
and tribal laws and regulations—along the entirety of the border violates the non-
delegation doctrine and Presentment Clause, art I, § 7. Supp. App. 61a–64a.6
During the week of August 3, 2026, Applicants began border barrier construc-
tion in Big Bend National Park without providing Respondents 30 days’ advance no-
tice, as had been agreed. D. Ct. Doc. 34 at 4. Respondents then moved for emergency
injunctive relief (the “Emergency Motion”) to enjoin border barrier construction and
associated activities within the Big Bend Sector pursuant to the Waivers until final
resolution on the merits. D. Ct. Doc. 34 at 20. On the same day, Applicants voluntarily
paused “all construction activity” in the National Park, a pause later described as
6

Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, U.S. Const. amend. V.

11
encompassing all of BBT-2 and BBT-4.7 D. Ct. Doc. 34 at 5; Supp. App. 256a. On
September 19, 2026, Respondents submitted supplemental evidence of then-ongoing
construction in BBT-1 and imminent construction in BBT-2 and/or 3. D. Ct. Doc. 55.
On September 21, 2026, with the voluntary “pause on ground disturbing activ-
ities in the Big Bend Sector” about to expire, the district court set a hearing on the
Emergency Motion. D. Ct. Doc. 56. The court ordered the parties to present evidence
regarding whether: (1) the Big Bend Sector is an “area of high illegal entry” within
the meaning of IIRIRA; (2) Plaintiffs were being irreparably harmed by ongoing con-
struction activity pursuant to the Waivers; (3) Plaintiffs would be irreparably harmed
by planned future construction; and (4) Defendants or the public interest would be
harmed by a preliminary injunction. Id. On September 29, 2026, Applicants reported
the end of the construction pause in BBT-2 and BBT-4. Supp. App. 257a.
At the evidentiary hearing on October 2, 2026, Respondents presented live tes-
timony from six fact witnesses and two expert witnesses, in addition to prior testi-
mony from a sheriff and former Customs and Border Protection officer. The govern-

REASONS TO DENY THE APPLICATION
I.
The District Court Correctly Held That Respondents Are Likely to Succeed
on Their Major Questions Doctrine Claim.
The major questions doctrine demands a clear congressional statement before
an executive body may assert authority over “decisions of vast economic and political
significance.” West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 716 (2022). The doctrine enforces
the Constitution’s allocation of legislative power to Congress by counseling skepti-
cism where an agency claims sweeping authority absent unmistakably clear text.
Here, the Secretary asserts newfound and extraordinary authority that he may in-
voke IIRIRA’s Section 102 waiver authority across the entirety of the southern bor-
der. See Supp. App. 114a. Under our Constitution, when confronted with decisions of
this magnitude, the question before the Court “is not whether something should be
done; it is who has the authority to do it.” Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477, 501 (2023);

14
see also Gonzales v. Oregon, 546 U.S. 243, 265 (2006) (the government’s sought after
authority was “inconsistent with the design of the statute”). Under the major ques-
tions doctrine, the decision of whether to waive laws across one-third of the border
for a cross-continental barrier, including areas that, as found by the district court,
involve the lowest border crossings by far, must be made by Congress, not the Exec-
utive. Failing to identify any clear congressional authorization for the power the Sec-
retary now claims, the Big Bend Waivers violate the major questions doctrine.
A.
The district court has jurisdiction over Respondents’ major questions
doctrine claim.
Section 102(c)(2)(A) of IIRIRA limits judicial review of waiver determinations
to causes of action or claims alleging a violation of the Constitution. Because the ma-
jor questions doctrine is, at its core, a constitutional doctrine designed to protect sep-
aration of powers, the district court correctly determined that it has jurisdiction to
resolve Respondents’ claim. App. 211a. This conclusion is supported by the doctrine’s
history and relationship to the nondelegation doctrine.
1.
At its inception, the major questions doctrine was born of “the hydraulic
pressures of our constitutional system” and the Court’s need to “rein in Congress’s
efforts to delegate legislative power.” Gundy v. United States, 588 U.S. 128, 166–67
(2019) (Gorsuch, J., joined by Roberts, C.J., and Thomas, J., dissenting). Operation-
ally, it works as a “dice-loading” clear statement rule, where something extrinsic to
the plain meaning of a statute’s text tips the scales towards a particular outcome. In
major questions cases, that extrinsic source is the Constitution. Learning Res., Inc.
v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 274 (2026) (Gorsuch, J., concurring).

15
A major questions doctrine claim does not merely allege that an agency mis-
read a statute. It is not, as Applicants allege, a statutory or ultra vires claim. See
Appl. at 14, 16 (characterizing major questions cases as simple statutory interpreta-
tion questions). Instead, a well-developed body of caselaw sets this doctrine apart
from more routine statutory violations. It alleges that an agency arrogated to itself
quintessential legislative power that the Constitution vests exclusively in Congress—
a claim that is constitutional at its core. See West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 735–36 (Gor-
such, J., joined by Alito, J., concurring). Indeed, the doctrine operates to interpret a
statutory grant of authority, but any contention that this feature is divorced from
constitutional underpinnings is misplaced.
2.
By way of analogy, the nondelegation doctrine implicates the same sep-
aration of powers safeguards, and similarly operates through statutory interpretation
to determine whether delegated authority is within constitutional bounds. See
Gundy, 588 U.S. at 135–36 (“[A] nondelegation inquiry always begins (and often al-
most ends) with statutory interpretation . . . Only after a court has determined a
challenged statute’s meaning can it decide whether the law sufficiently guides exec-
utive discretion to accord with Article I.”). That a doctrine is effectuated through stat-
utory interpretation and probes a grant of authority does not change its constitutional
source or purpose.
In effectuating Article I, the nondelegation and major questions doctrines are
two sides of the same coin—“[b]oth are designed to protect the separation of powers”
and to ensure that new authorities affecting the lives of Americans “are subject to the

16
robust democratic processes the Constitution demands.” Nat’l Fed’n of Indep. Bus. v.
DOL, OSHA, 595 U.S. 109, 124 (2022) (Gorsuch, J., joined by Thomas & Alito, J.J.,
concurring); see also Learning Res., 607 U.S. at 284 (Gorsuch, J., concurring) (“Like
the nondelegation doctrine, the major questions doctrine protects Article I’s Vesting
Clause . . .”). Both doctrines enforce an affirmative constitutional prohibition against
overexpansive delegations of Congress’s legislative power. In this way, major ques-
tions is best described as an “as-applied nondelegation doctrine” which allows courts
to “hold that the [executive action], rather than the statute, violates the Constitu-
tion.” Ilan Wurman, The Specification Power, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 689, 730 (2020).8
3.
Nothing in Respondents’ claim or the major questions precedent on
which Respondents rely is in tension with Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462 (1994).
Dalton stands for the unremarkable proposition that not “every action by the Presi-
dent, or by another executive official, in excess of his statutory authority is ipso facto
in violation of the Constitution.” Id. at 472 (emphasis added). Respondents’ position
is not to the contrary. Rather, the claim put forth, and preliminarily accepted by the
district court, is a narrow one: the decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and
tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure,

As the district court reasoned, if everywhere along the nearly 2,000-mile border qualifies as

truly “extraordinary” assertion of power. See West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 723.
Under our tripartite system of government, such sweeping assertions of power
must be decided by Congress. That the Secretary has usurped such power for himself,
in the absence of a clear delegation, violates the Constitution. “And without doctrines
like major questions, our system of separated powers and checks-and-balances
threatens to give way to the continual and permanent accretion of power in the hands
of one man. That is no recipe for a republic.” Learning Res., 607 U.S. at 270–71 (Gor-

C. Congress did not clearly authorize the Big Bend Waivers.
1.
The district court found that Big Bend is, “by far, the sector with the

The district court’s analysis is entirely consistent with this Court’s precedent.
When assessing an extraordinary assertion of authority, a court should be “reluctant
to read into ambiguous statutory text the delegation claimed to be lurking there.”
West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 723 (cleaned up). Thus, “clear congressional authorization”
is necessary. Id. Here, Applicants point to IIRIRA for authority to waive laws across
the Big Bend Sector, but the statute grants no such authority.

statutory safeguards across the entire border, including in areas that have, by far,
the lowest rates of unlawful entry. See Biden, 600 U.S. at 500 (holding that the HE-

IV.
The District Court’s Preliminary Ruling Does Not Warrant Certiorari.
The government’s request that the Court treat its application as a petition for
a writ of certiorari and “summarily reverse the district court’s order,” Appl. at 35–36,
should be denied. The government cites no relevant precedent to support that

38
extreme request.17 In any event, the district court’s preliminary ruling does not war-
rant this Court’s review, much less summary reversal.
First, there is no conflict with any other ruling because none of the other dis-
trict court decisions upholding different waiver decisions were presented with, or ad-
dressed, a major questions issue. Nor has any other court held an evidentiary hear-
ing, considered extensive evidence including fact and expert testimony, and then
made specific factual findings that the area for which basic legal safeguards have
been waived is “in ‘extraordinarily distant last place’ for apprehensions” along the
entire southern border. App. 213a. Consequently, this Court’s review, at least at this
preliminary juncture, is unnecessary to resolve any conflict in the lower courts.
Second, a preliminary injunction decision is, in any case, a poor vehicle for this
Court’s review. The district court’s final ruling on the pending summary judgment
motions may alter or refine the court’s reasoning on the major questions doctrine as
well as resolve Respondents’ additional constitutional claims that are directly related
to application of the major questions doctrine. See Abbott v. Veasey, 580 U.S. 1104,
1105 (2017) (Roberts, C.J., statement respecting denial of certiorari) (explaining that
the “District Court has yet to enter a final remedial order” and that the “issues will
be better suited for certiorari review at that time”).
17

authorize a single Executive Branch official to waive compliance with a vast array of

grave nondelegation concerns. If “areas of high entry” literally means everywhere—

apply anywhere along the nearly 2,000-mile Southern border (or, for that matter, the
entire Northern border) would mean that Congress has delegated its “[c]ore legisla-

Third, the extent to which the major questions doctrine presents a constitu-

note. The government does not identify any other statutes with the same or compa-

any other pressing need for the Court to provide further guidance to lower courts
regarding the constitutional dimensions of the major questions doctrine. That the
government disagrees with the preliminary legal reasoning of the district court is an
insufficient reason to grant certiorari.
Finally, there is also no compelling practical reason for the Court to grant re-
view at this juncture. As explained, the parties have already filed summary judgment
briefing with the district court; border apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector have
fallen to historic lows even without invocation of IIRIRA’s waiver authority; and the
preliminary injunction simply requires DHS to comply with the same laws that apply
to other agency actions throughout the country.

The Court should deny the government’s application.
